A computing paradigm where digital media and applications blend seamlessly into physical 3D space, navigated via eye tracking, hand gestures, and voice
A computer designed exclusively for calculating spacecraft orbits
10.explanation: Spatial computing (e.g. Apple Vision Pro) breaks free of physical glass screens, transforming the user's surrounding physical room into an infinite workspace.

10.question: What does 'Open Source' software licensing (e.g. GNU GPL, MIT License) grant to developers and designers?
options: A guarantee that the software will never contain bugs
The legal freedom to view, modify, distribute, and build upon the underlying computer source code freely and collaboratively
The right to use copyrighted artwork without giving credit
Free computer hardware provided by governments
10.explanation: Open source software (e.g. Blender, Godot, Linux) fosters collaborative innovation, transparent security, and community-driven creative power.

10.question: What is 'Digital Rights Management' (DRM)?
options: A systematic access-control technology used by publishers and copyright holders to limit the unauthorized copying, sharing, and use of digital media files
A software program that makes audio files play louder
A government human rights agency for digital artists
A legal permit required to operate a YouTube channel
10.explanation: DRM applies encryption and hardware locks to restrict piracy, though critics argue it frustrates legitimate paying consumers and preservationists.

10.question: What is 'Native Advertising' (Sponsored Content)?
options: Advertisements for indigenous tourist attractions
Advertisements displayed on physical outdoor billboards
A type of paid advertising that matches the visual form, tone, and editorial style of the publication or platform in which it appears (disguised as regular editorial)
Advertisements printed on physical paper newspapers
10.explanation: Native ads blend into editorial feeds seamlessly, requiring clear ethical labeling ('Sponsored', 'Paid Ad') to avoid deceiving readers.

10.question: What is 'Clickbait' in digital journalism and media headlines?
options: Sensationalized, exaggerated, or misleading headlines designed to exploit curiosity and manipulate users into clicking, often leading to underwhelming content
A technique used to repair broken computer mice
A tool used to catch fish using computer sensors
A software button that increases internet connection speed
10.explanation: Clickbait exploits cognitive curiosity gaps to drive ad revenue impressions, degrading journalistic integrity and reader trust.

10.question: What is 'Media Literacy' and why is it considered an indispensable 21st-century skill?
options: The ability to access, critically analyze, evaluate, and create media in diverse forms, distinguishing credible facts from bias, propaganda, and synthetic deception
Having a social media account with many followers
The ability to read and write in the English language
Knowing how to operate an expensive cinema camera
10.explanation: Media literacy empowers citizens to critically interrogate authorship, motives, representation, and synthetic authenticity in the digital age.

10.question: What is the 'Right of Publicity' (Personality Rights)?
options: The legal right of an individual to control the commercial use of their name, image, likeness, voice, or distinctive identity
The right to become a famous social media influencer
The right to give public speeches in city parks
The right to have your name published in daily newspapers
10.explanation: Personality rights protect individuals from having their face or voice commercialized without permission, vital in the era of AI voice/likeness clones.

10.question: What is 'Photogrammetry' in digital media and 3D asset creation?
options: Measuring camera shutter speed using laser beams
Printing physical photographs on canvas fabric
Developing analog photographic film in a darkroom
The science and technology of reconstructing accurate 3D models and textures from multiple overlapping 2D photographs taken around a real-world object or landscape
10.explanation: Photogrammetry digitizes reality: processing hundreds of camera angles into photorealistic 3D scans for cinema VFX and game worlds.

10.question: What is 'Volumetric Video' (Holographic Video)?
options: A video file that takes up zero storage space
Capturing real-world moving performances from all angles in full 3D space, allowing viewers to watch the live action from any vantage point in VR/AR
A traditional 2D video played on a wide curved screen
A video recorded at very high audio volume
10.explanation: Volumetric capture turns real human acting into living, explorable 3D holograms that users can walk around inside virtual space.

10.question: What is 'Prompt Engineering' in the context of Generative AI tools?
options: Writing binary machine code for computer processors
Repairing broken camera optical zoom lenses
The iterative art and skill of structuring, refining, and designing natural language text prompts to guide AI models into producing desired creative outputs
Building physical computer engines for automobiles
10.explanation: Prompt engineering combines semantic vocabulary, stylistic modifiers, parameters, and artistic references to steer AI outputs accurately.

10.question: What is the 'Uncanny Valley' in robotics, animation, and CGI?
options: A psychological phenomenon where near-human replications that appear almost, but not quite, completely realistic evoke feelings of revulsion and eerie discomfort in viewers
A geological canyon where film cameras are tested
A valley where digital film production studios are built
A software bug that turns animated characters upside down
10.explanation: Coined by Masahiro Mori, the uncanny valley marks the dip in emotional affinity when CGI humans look subtly dead-eyed or unnatural.

10.question: What is 'In-App Purchasing' (Microtransactions) in mobile app monetization ethics?
options: Buying physical groceries using a mobile phone app
Paying a one-time fee to download a commercial computer software

Selling virtual goods, cosmetics, or premium gameplay features inside an application, which raises ethical concerns regarding predatory exploitation of children and gambling-like mechanics (loot boxes)
Purchasing a smartphone at a retail electronics store
10.explanation: Microtransactions and variable-ratio loot boxes exploit psychological vulnerabilities, leading to strict regulatory scrutiny in several countries.

10.question: What is 'Shadowbanning' on social media platforms?
options: Blocking sunlight from hitting computer monitors
A legal penalty for copyright infringement
The covert practice of blocking or reducing the visibility of a user's content to the community without notifying the user that they have been restricted
Banning users who post dark black-and-white photos
10.explanation: Shadowbanning suppresses engagement secretly, provoking debates over platform transparency, censorship, and free speech.

10.question: What is the 'Panopticon' metaphor applied to modern digital surveillance capitalism?
options: A security guard who watches television all day
An optical lens that captures panoramic photographs
A museum exhibiting historical computers
A state of pervasive, continuous digital tracking and surveillance where individuals modify their behavior because they never know when they are being watched or monetized
10.explanation: Originating with Jeremy Bentham and Michel Foucault, the panopticon illustrates how constant data harvesting shapes societal behavior.

10.question: What is 'Copyright Infringement' versus 'Plagiarism'?
options: Copyright infringement is minor; Plagiarism is a criminal offense punishable by prison
Copyright infringement applies to words; Plagiarism applies to images
Copyright infringement is a legal violation of exclusive intellectual property rights; Plagiarism is an ethical and academic violation of passing off another's ideas as one's own without attribution
There is zero functional difference between them
10.explanation: Plagiarism violates academic honesty (stealing ideas/words without credit); copyright infringement violates statutory property law (unauthorized reproduction).

10.question: What is 'Watermarking' in digital image asset management?
options: Soaking physical photographic prints in chemical water baths
A watermark defect caused by rain on camera lenses
Embedding a visible or invisible digital pattern, logo, or cryptographic signature into an image to identify ownership and protect copyright
An artistic watercolor painting effect applied to photos
10.explanation: Watermarking brands previews or embeds forensic steganographic data to trace unauthorized leaks and commercial use.

10.question: What does 'User Consent' require under ethical data design standards?
options: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, and granted through a clear affirmative action without deceptive pre-ticked boxes
Consent is assumed automatically whenever a user visits a website
Consent is permanent and can never be withdrawn by the user
Consent requires a signed letter delivered by postal mail
10.explanation: Ethical consent prohibits coercive dark patterns, ensuring users retain genuine, transparent control over their private data.

10.question: What is 'Spatial Audio' and 'Dolby Atmos' in contemporary cinema and streaming?
options: A sound effect produced by lightning strikes
An audio format that only works on headphones
A physical theater with very loud speakers
An object-based sound technology where audio elements are treated as independent 3D sound objects positioned and moved dynamically anywhere in a 3D hemisphere, including overhead
10.explanation: Unlike channel-based 5.1/7.1, Dolby Atmos maps audio to 3D coordinates, rendering precisely across any speaker array with height dimensions.

10.question: What is the overarching ethical responsibility of a Digital Media Designer in the 21st century?
options: To generate maximum advertising revenue at the expense of user mental health
To replace human creativity entirely with automated artificial intelligence
To ensure every digital design project wins international design awards
To create inclusive, truthful, accessible, and human-centered media experiences that enrich culture, respect user autonomy, and promote societal well-being
10.explanation: Designers shape human perception, behavior, and democratic discourse; their ultimate duty is designing with integrity, empathy, and ethical conscience.
